newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian decree sees state stake in indebted firms.
newsitem.headline: Russian decree sees state stake in indebted firms.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin has signed a resolution ordering indebted enterprises to transfer controlling stakes in trust to the state or face bankruptcy, a government spokeswoman said on Wednesday.
Larisa Zelkova, spokeswoman for First Deputy Prime Minister Vladimir Potanin, told Reuters that the scheme was part of a broad government plan to restructure companies' state debts.
Firms with large tax arrears not wishing to participate in the scheme would be turned over to the Federal Bankruptcy Agency, she said.
Under the scheme, indebted companies would transfer 50 percent plus one share of their paper equity to the Federal Property Fund.
In return, companies would win a five year reprieve in which to pay off their principal debt and 10 years to pay off fines.
If during the restructuring period a company failed to make two consecutive payments or stopped paying current taxes, the state could sell the shares.
Zelkova said the state would hold the shares in trust for 10 years.
The government would accept shares owned by other entities with stakes in the companies or newly-issued shares, she said.
If a company could not issue new shares, it would have to issue property-backed bonds. In such a case, debt principle would be restructured over two years and fines over five years.
Zelkova said a list of companies in need of debt restructuring had not yet been drawn up, but she said Russia's biggest car company AvtoVAZ would be at the top of the list.
AvtoVAZ's debt to the state is about 2.9 trillion roubles.

Tax shortfalls are one of the most acute economic problems in Russia, and low collection levels have several times prevented the International Monetary Fund from paying tranches of its $10 billion, three-year loan.
Official figures show that tax arrears had doubled year-on-year to 128.25 trillion roubles at the start of 1997.

Companies argue that they cannot afford to pay taxes while they are owed money for deliveries. The government, especially state-owned plants in the military-industrial complex, is one of the biggest non-payers.
